chapter: The Lunceford years: Europe, rivals and bandsmen
title: Tommy Dorsey and circular breathing
summary: Crawford admires Tommy Dorsey's smooth tone and breath control, which Sinatra noticed.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: What did you all think of -- did you like any of the white bands that were playing during the '30s?
Dorsey, Goodman. That was a sweet trombone player, wasn't he?
Oh, yeah. Buh-duh-duh-duh-duh-duh-uh uh, da-da-da-da-da-da-da-a-a-a, I'm getting [crossed out: sick and tired] [inserted: constantly] -- I know he played, sound much better than I singing, but --

-- but just a little taste of it. Oh, that Dorsey was a smoothie. Yeah, he used to hold those notes, blowing. There's a word for it, playing, do all that, and still notes down and even and pretty as a picture, inhaling and exhaling at the same time.
That's what he -- man, he was famous
for that. And he wouldn't let nobody know. Frank Sinatra noticed that man. Frank said, how he could do it is unbelievable. Tommy Dorsey.
